```{r setup, include=FALSE}
set.seed(486649)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
  fig.align = "center", fig.pos = "H", out.width = "78%",

library(knitr); library(kableExtra)
find_data <- function(f) {
  cands <- c(file.path("../../../processed_data", f),
             file.path("processed_data", f), f)
  hit <- cands[file.exists(cands)]
  if (!length(hit)) stop("Not found: ", f); hit[1]
}

c1  <- read.csv(find_data("10_analysis1_coefs.csv"))
a2  <- read.csv(find_data("12_analysis2_auc_by_landmark.csv"))
gm  <- read.csv(find_data("13_analysis3_gee.csv"))
cx  <- read.csv(find_data("13_analysis3_tvcox.csv"))
ut  <- read.csv(find_data("15_analysis4_utility.csv"))
al  <- read.csv(find_data("15_analysis4_alarm_sweep.csv"))
sg  <- read.csv(find_data("16_analysis5_subgroups.csv"))

en_auc <- m1$auroc[m1$model == "Analysis1 full-feature elastic net"]
p1_auc <- m1$auroc[grepl("0.755", m1$model)]
alpha <- gm$OR_glm[gm$term == "__alpha_within_patient__"]
se_infl_max <- max(gm$SE_inflation, na.rm = TRUE)
best_u <- ut[which.max(ut$utility_norm), ]
op90 <- al[which.min(abs(al$sensitivity - 0.90)), ]
op50 <- al[which.min(abs(al$sensitivity - 0.50)), ]
K6 <- length(unique(gm6$class))
psm_row <- ce[ce$method == "PSM (1:1 nearest, ATT)", ]
ipw_row <- ce[ce$method == "IPW (ATE weights)", ]
aipw_row <- ce[ce$method == "AIPW / doubly robust (ATE)", ]
```

# Objective and prior results

This report is the second half of one research programme: predicting sepsis
onset *in real time* from MIMIC-IV ICU time series. The earlier stage
(scripts 01-09) built the temporal substrate: a 3.1M-row hourly panel, an
hourly Sepsis-3 onset label, and a leakage-safe hour-6 landmark cohort of
`r format(a2$n_at_risk[a2$landmark_h==6], big.mark=",")` at-risk stays. A
multivariable hourly logistic model reached a cross-validated AUROC of
**`r sprintf("%.3f", p1_auc)`** for incident onset within 12 h,
out-discriminating SOFA, qSOFA and SIRS. This report builds the real-time
model itself and closes two gaps identified in comparable MIMIC-IV studies:
group-based trajectory modelling (GBTM) and propensity-based confounder
adjustment. All seven analyses are built **entirely from classical statistics**
(no gradient boosting, no neural sequence models), reaching real-time
prediction through **dynamic landmarking** (van Houwelingen 2007).

# Analysis 1: statistical ceiling (full-feature nomogram at hour 6)

The earlier multivariable model used only non-circular predictors and, because
plain complete-case regression cannot use the 70-88%-missing labs at hour 6,
effectively dropped them. Analysis 1 lifts both restrictions with an elastic-net
penalised logistic model over the full feature set. The missing labs are handled
by an **informative-missingness design** (median imputation plus a "was it
measured" indicator per lab and per trajectory slope). Evaluation is
patient-grouped 5-fold CV with the penalty strength chosen by inner
cross-validation on each training fold.

```{r t1tab}
m1d <- m1
m1d$delong_p_vs_baseline_traj <- ifelse(is.na(m1d$delong_p_vs_baseline_traj),
   "-", formatC(m1d$delong_p_vs_baseline_traj, format="e", digits=1))
kable(m1d, booktabs = TRUE, col.names = c("Model","AUROC","PR-AUC","Brier","DeLong p vs 0.755"),
      caption = "Discrimination at the hour-6 landmark (out-of-sample). The full-feature elastic net is the purely-statistical ceiling.") %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position","scale_down"))
```

The full-feature model reaches AUROC **`r sprintf("%.3f", en_auc)`**, a
statistically significant gain over the earlier `r sprintf("%.3f", p1_auc)`
model (DeLong *p* `r format.pval(m1$delong_p_vs_baseline_traj[nrow(m1)], digits=2, eps=1e-16)`),
with improved PR-AUC. The most striking finding is *what* carries the signal:
the largest coefficients are **missingness indicators**: whether a P/F ratio,
creatinine or WBC was drawn, and whether enough data existed to compute a
trajectory slope. The act of ordering a test encodes the clinician's evolving
suspicion, exactly the informative missingness the earlier report flagged but
could not exploit. Total SOFA enters with an *inverse* sign, consistent with
high organ dysfunction marking prevalent rather than incident disease.

```{r t1coef}
top <- c1[order(-abs(c1$coef)), ]; top <- top[top$term != "(Intercept)", ][1:10, ]
kable(top, booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
      col.names = c("Feature","Coefficient","Odds ratio"),
      caption = "Ten largest standardized effects in the Analysis-1 model (\\_msg = measurement indicator).") %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position")
```

The result stops short of the 0.80-0.83 the README projected: at a 6-hour
landmark the labs that would lift discrimination are mostly not yet drawn, so
their imputed values add little beyond the fact of their absence.
`r sprintf("%d", nrow(c1)-1)` of the 27 candidate features survive penalization.

# Analysis 2: real-time deliverable (dynamic landmark supermodel)

A single landmark answers "predict from hour 6." A deployed system must predict
at *every* hour. The classical solution is a **landmark supermodel**: the
landmark construction is repeated on a grid of prediction hours *s* in
{6,12,18,24,36,48}, stacked, and fit as one penalised model with landmark time
*s*, $s^2$ and feature-by-*s* interactions, so evaluation at the current hour
yields an hourly-updating risk. Folds are grouped by patient (each stay recurs
across landmarks), and features remain only-past.

```{r t2tab}
kable(a2, booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
      col.names = c("Landmark hour s","At risk","Onset in 12h","AUROC supermodel","AUROC separate"),
      caption = "Dynamic discrimination AUC(s): one supermodel evaluated at each prediction hour, versus fitting a separate model per landmark.") %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position")
```

```{r auc-s, fig.cap="AUC(s): the supermodel's out-of-sample discrimination as a function of the hour at which the prediction is made, versus per-landmark models.", out.width="62%"}
include_graphics(fig("12_auc_by_landmark.png"))
```

The single supermodel matches the accuracy of a bespoke model at every
prediction hour while remaining one parsimonious, deployable object.
Discrimination is highest early (AUROC
`r sprintf("%.2f", a2$auc_supermodel[a2$landmark_h==6])` at hour 6), dips in the
mid-stay window (hours 18-24) where incident onset is rarest and hardest, and
recovers later. This *is* the real-time model, produced entirely within the
classical statistics domain.

# Analysis 3: within-patient correlation

The earlier analysis did not address the correlation among repeated hourly rows
from one patient. Two classical repeated-measures tools close that gap on the
sampled panel, using incident onset within 12 h (evaluated only on at-risk
hours) as the dynamic outcome. A per-patient random-intercept GLMM is
*degenerate* here: most patients never have an event, so their intercepts
diverge. The population-averaged route is used instead.

A **GEE** with exchangeable working correlation estimates within-patient
correlation at **`r sprintf("%.2f", alpha)`**: hourly observations within a
patient are strongly dependent, so the effective information is far below the
`r format(76538, big.mark=",")` row count. **Cluster-robust (sandwich) standard
errors** on the pooled logistic model inflate the SEs by up to
**`r sprintf("%.1fx", se_infl_max)`** compared to naive model-based SEs that
assume independent hours. Without this correction, a pooled GLM would report
spuriously tight confidence intervals. A ridge-penalised
**time-varying-covariate Cox** model on the counting-process form gives
directionally consistent instantaneous hazards of onset:

```{r t3tab-gee}
gtab <- gm[gm$term != "__alpha_within_patient__", ]
kable(gtab, booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
      col.names = c("Term","OR","SE naive","SE cluster-robust","SE inflation"),
      caption = "Pooled logistic model: naive vs cluster-robust (by patient) standard errors. Ignoring within-patient correlation understates every SE.") %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position")
```

```{r t3tab-cox}
cx$direction <- ifelse(cx$HR > 1, "raises hazard", "lowers hazard")
kable(cx, booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
      col.names = c("Covariate (standardized)","Hazard ratio","Interpretation"),
      caption = "Ridge time-varying Cox: hazard of incident onset per SD of the evolving vital.") %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position")
```

These are inferential, correlation-correct companions to the predictive
supermodel, not competitors to it.

# Analysis 4: real-time evaluation (utility and alarm burden)

Discrimination alone is insufficient for a streaming alarm. The supermodel emits
an hourly risk on a held-out 6,000-stay set (trained on the remainder, no
leakage), scored at every hour from hour 6 to onset or discharge.

The **PhysioNet/CinC-2019 utility score**, which rewards early detection and
penalises both late and false alarms, is maximised at
**`r sprintf("%.3f", best_u$utility_norm)`** (normalised: 0 = never alarm,
1 = per-hour oracle) at a risk threshold of `r sprintf("%.2f", best_u$threshold)`.
A positive score confirms the model adds value over silence on this
incident-only ICU task.

The clinically decisive picture is the **alarm burden**:

```{r t4tab}
show <- al[al$threshold %in% c(op90$threshold, al$threshold[which.min(abs(al$sensitivity-0.7))], op50$threshold), ]
kable(show, booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
      col.names = c("Threshold","Sensitivity","False alarms / patient-day","Frac. non-septic pts alarmed"),
      caption = "Operating points: earlier/more-sensitive detection costs rapidly rising false-alarm burden.") %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position")
```

```{r alarm, fig.cap="Sensitivity versus false-alarm burden for the real-time supermodel. High sensitivity is reachable only at an alarm rate that would fatigue bedside staff.", out.width="62%"}
include_graphics(fig("15_alarm_tradeoff.png"))
```

Catching 90% of septic patients in a timely window costs about
**`r sprintf("%.1f", op90$fa_per_patient_day)` false alarms per patient-day**,
firing on `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100*op90$frac_nonseptic_pts_alarmed)` of
non-septic patients: untenable alarm fatigue. A calmer operating point
(`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100*op50$sensitivity)` sensitivity) drops that to
`r sprintf("%.1f", op50$fa_per_patient_day)` per patient-day. This is the
number a deployment decision actually turns on.

# Analysis 5: subgroup fairness

Within MIMIC-IV, the Analysis-1 risk is well calibrated and similarly discriminating
across sex and age bands. A model can discriminate well overall yet fail a
subgroup; that is not the case here.

```{r t5tab}
kable(sg, booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
      col.names = c("Subgroup","n","Event rate","AUROC","Mean pred.","Obs. rate","Calib. ratio"),
      caption = "Subgroup discrimination and calibration-in-the-large (ratio near 1.0 = well calibrated).") %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position","scale_down"))
```

# Analysis 6: group-based trajectory modelling (GBTM)

Comparable MIMIC-IV studies (Yang et al. 2022) use **group-based trajectory
modelling** to summarise repeated SOFA scores into latent trajectory classes
and link membership to mortality via Cox regression. The earlier temporal
report used a within-patient HMM, which clusters *states within one patient*
rather than *trajectory shapes across patients*. Analysis 6 fits a latent-class
growth model (flexmix grouped-mixture-of-regressions) to first-24h SOFA
trajectories on the sampled panel (2,438 stays with sufficient repeated
observations), selecting `r K6` classes by BIC.

```{r gbtm-fig, fig.cap="GBTM: latent SOFA-trajectory classes over the first 24 ICU hours.", out.width="62%"}
include_graphics(fig("18_gbtm_trajectories.png"))
```

Class membership shows a strong, monotonic dose-response relationship with
both outcomes, exactly as Yang et al.'s design intends:

```{r t6cox}
kable(gc, booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
      col.names = c("Term","Hazard ratio","p-value"),
      caption = "Cox model: in-hospital mortality by GBTM trajectory class (reference = mildest class), adjusted for age.") %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position")
```

```{r t6onset}
kable(go, booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
      col.names = c("Term","Odds ratio","p-value"),
      caption = "Logistic model: incident Sepsis-3 by GBTM trajectory class (reference = mildest class); this project's own outcome of interest, beyond Yang et al.'s mortality-only design.") %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position")
```

The steeply-worsening trajectory class carries several-fold higher mortality
and Sepsis-3 risk than the mild, flat class: the SOFA trajectory *shape*,
not just its hour-24 endpoint, is informative, consistent with the
project's broader finding that dynamics carry signal a snapshot misses.

# Analysis 7: confounder-adjusted causal analysis

Every prior analysis reports an *association* (a risk score, a hazard ratio).
Following the causal-adjustment designs of Guo et al. (2025) and Zou et al.
(2022), Analysis 7 applies **propensity score matching (PSM)**, **inverse
probability weighting (IPW)**, and **doubly robust estimation** to estimate a
confounder-adjusted treatment effect. The question: does administering
antibiotics within 3 h of ICU admission (the Surviving Sepsis Campaign's
"hour-3 bundle" threshold) lower in-hospital mortality among Sepsis-3 patients,
after adjusting for baseline severity and case-mix? Sicker patients may be
treated faster, or slower if sepsis is not yet recognised, so a naive comparison
is biased in an unknown direction.

The adjustment set is chosen by **LASSO** from age, sex, admission type, ICU
type, race, and the six SOFA organ components; all 11 candidates survived
penalisation. Four estimators of increasing robustness are compared:

```{r t7tab}
kable(ce, booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
      col.names = c("Method","Estimand","Risk diff.","RD 95% CI low","RD 95% CI high",
                    "Odds ratio","OR 95% CI low","OR 95% CI high"),
      caption = "Effect of early (<=3h) vs delayed antibiotics on in-hospital mortality, Sepsis-3 cohort.") %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position","scale_down"))
```

```{r t7fig, fig.cap="Covariate balance (standardized mean difference) before and after propensity-score matching.", out.width="70%"}
include_graphics(fig("19_analysis7_balance_love_plot.png"))
```

Matching brings every covariate's standardized mean difference below the
conventional 0.1 threshold (figure above). All four estimators (crude,
PSM, IPW, and the doubly robust augmented-IPW estimator, consistent if
*either* the propensity model *or* the outcome model is correctly specified)
agree in direction and magnitude: early antibiotics associate with lower
mortality (PSM OR `r sprintf("%.3f", psm_row$odds_ratio)`, 95% CI
`r sprintf("%.3f", psm_row$or_ci_low)`-`r sprintf("%.3f", psm_row$or_ci_high)`;
IPW OR `r sprintf("%.3f", ipw_row$odds_ratio)`, 95% CI
`r sprintf("%.3f", ipw_row$or_ci_low)`-`r sprintf("%.3f", ipw_row$or_ci_high)`;
doubly robust risk difference `r sprintf("%.3f", aipw_row$risk_difference)`,
95% CI `r sprintf("%.3f", aipw_row$rd_ci_low)` to
`r sprintf("%.3f", aipw_row$rd_ci_high)`). Agreement across four estimators
built on different assumptions is the strongest evidence this pipeline offers
for the finding being a real association rather than residual confounding,
though, as an observational analysis, it cannot rule out unmeasured
confounders (e.g. severity-of-illness trends not captured by day-1 SOFA).

# Conclusion

This report reaches the project's real-time goal entirely within classical
statistics. A **full-feature nomogram** sets the discrimination ceiling
(AUROC `r sprintf("%.3f", en_auc)`), with informative measurement patterns
dominating the signal. A **dynamic landmark supermodel** delivers one
interpretable, hourly-updating risk that matches per-landmark models across
the stay. **GEE and time-varying Cox** correct the within-patient correlation
the earlier analysis ignored (within-patient correlation
`r sprintf("%.2f", alpha)`, cluster-robust SEs up to
`r sprintf("%.1fx", se_infl_max)` the naive ones). A **utility- and
alarm-based evaluation** exposes the real cost of a sensitive alarm. **GBTM**
shows that the shape of a patient's SOFA trajectory, not just its level,
predicts both mortality and incident sepsis. A **PSM/IPW/doubly robust**
causal analysis finds a consistent, confounder-adjusted mortality benefit for
early antibiotics across four estimators. The discrimination ceiling is set by
the label's dependence on clinician recognition, not by model class.
